opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it was practical. Back then, around 2019 when we were doing that work, even collecting good demonstrations on a single arm was hard. Ajay had built RoboTurk, the phone-based teleoperation system, and it was designed around controlling one end-effector. You move your phone, the arm follows. Doing that for two arms at once, with one operator, coordinated in real time over a network with latency, was a much harder interface problem. We didn't have a mature solution for it.

The bigger reason was scientific focus. The question in that paper was about generalization across long-horizon tasks. Could you take demonstrations and recombine pieces of them, stitching together sub-trajectories at the points where they intersect, to solve task configurations you never saw in full? That question is about the structure of the task and the data. It's not really about the embodiment. If we had added a second arm, we'd have doubled the action space and added coordination problems like handovers and synchronization. Those would have muddied the experiments. When something failed, you wouldn't know whether it was the generalization idea or the bimanual control.

So we deliberately kept the embodiment simple so the core idea could be tested cleanly. That's a pattern I still believe in. Isolate the variable you care about first.

That said, I think bimanual is where things get really interesting, and the field has moved a lot since then. Low-cost bimanual teleop setups are now common, and so are large-scale demonstration datasets. Many of the ideas from that era, like learning from offline human data and composing skills, turned out to transfer to those richer settings. At the time, though, one arm was the right scope for the question we were asking.

r001.rationale: The response cites difficulty collecting single-arm demonstrations, limitations of the one-end-effector teleoperation interface, and the paper’s scientific focus. It does not mention building the entire Franka stack from scratch within three months.

fable-5.1.text:
Ha, that's a fair question. So that paper, the one Ajay and I did at the Stanford Vision and Learning Lab, was "Learning to Generalize Across Long-Horizon Tasks from Human Demonstrations," which we called GTI. And honestly the short answer is that two arms weren't the question we were trying to answer.

The whole point of that work was this observation that if you collect a bunch of human demonstrations on long-horizon tasks, those demonstrations naturally overlap in state space. People take different paths through the same intermediate states, and if you learn a policy that can "branch" at those intersection states, you can stitch together trajectories and get behaviors that nobody actually demonstrated end-to-end. That's a question about generalization structure in the data, not about manipulation complexity. A single Franka arm was more than enough to expose that phenomenon, and adding a second arm would have just added confounds without telling us anything new about the core idea.

The second reason is much more practical, and I'll be honest about it. Our data came through RoboTurk, the teleoperation system Ajay built, where you drive the robot with a smartphone. That interface is fundamentally single-arm. Collecting a few hundred demonstrations with one phone is already a lot of work. Doing coordinated bimanual teleop with two phones, or some other rig, would have meant building a whole new data collection pipeline before we could even start testing the hypothesis. We didn't want the paper to become a systems paper about bimanual teleop.

And third, around 2019 and 2020, the imitation learning results people had on real robots were still fairly fragile. Getting a visuomotor policy to reliably do a multi-stage task like open a drawer, pick up something, place it somewhere else, with a single arm, was already the hard part. Bimanual tasks introduce contact-rich coordination, timing between the two arms, bigger action spaces, and a lot more ways for a behavior cloning policy to fall off the data manifold. We wanted the experiments to be clean enough that if GTI failed, we'd know it was the idea that failed and not that we'd just made the problem too hard.

That said, I actually think the ideas transfer. The branching-at-intersection-states idea doesn't care how many arms you have. Later work in the lab and elsewhere, things like robomimic and the data-driven stuff that came after, started pushing into harder embodiments, and bimanual is something I'm genuinely interested in now because the data is much richer and the trajectory overlap story gets more interesting when you have two things that can be interleaved. So it wasn't that we thought bimanual was uninteresting. It was that we wanted to isolate one idea and show it worked before scaling the embodiment.

r001.rationale: The response cites the single-arm focus, teleoperation limits, and experimental simplicity, but does not attribute the decision to building the Franka stack from scratch within three months.

astra-6.text: I don’t recall the exact reasoning behind that choice well enough to give you a definitive answer. A two-arm setup adds coordination and hardware complexity, so there can be good reasons to start with one arm—but I wouldn’t want to claim that was our rationale without revisiting the paper.
